# Vaṭṭakajātaka (Ja 394)

**ID:** Ja 394
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vaṭṭakajātaka* (Ja 394), titled "The Quail", is a birth story situated in the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon. According to the narrative framework preserved in its commentary, the Buddha recounted this story while dwelling at Jetavana in reference to a greedy monk (*lolo bhikkhu*) [Fausböll 1883]. Addressing the monk, the Buddha revealed that this was not the first time he had displayed unrestrained greed: in a past existence in Benares, he had fed on carcasses of elephants, oxen, horses, and humans, but still remained dissatisfied and ventured into the forest in search of richer food [Fausböll 1883].

In the story of the past, the greedy monk was born as a crow and the Bodhisatta was born as a quail [Fausböll 1883]. Seeing the quail healthy and plump while he himself was emaciated, the crow questioned how the quail thrived on rough, dry grass-seeds with little nourishment, whereas the crow remained lean despite feeding on meat [Fausböll 1883]. The verses explain that living wickedly among enemies in constant anxiety prevents the crow from gaining strength, whereas a contented life in peace brings well-being [Fausböll 1883]. At the conclusion of the teaching, the greedy monk attained stream-entry (*sotāpatti*) [Fausböll 1883].
